questions.prompt: In Salesforce, what is a record type used for, as applied in the Harrow Industrial Supply sales-redesign case?
options: Giving one object different picklist values, required fields, and page layouts per business process, without creating separate objects
Granting a group of users additional access to records on top of the organization-wide default
Setting the baseline record-level access for an object before any sharing mechanism adds to it
Automatically giving a manager visibility into the records owned by the people below them
questions.explain: A record type lets one object (like Opportunity) carry different stages, required fields, and layouts per segment or process, while all records stay in the same object for unified reporting — exactly how Harrow's three sales segments were handled on one Opportunity object.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a sharing rule, not a record type. A sharing rule is the separate mechanism that answers who can see a record; a record type answers what shape that record's process takes. The two solve different problems even though both get configured on the same object, which is the core distinction Lesson 1 draws.

questions.prompt: Why did this course recommend starting Harrow's Opportunity organization-wide default (OWD) at Private rather than something more open?
options: Widening OWD later is comparatively low-risk, while tightening it later forces re-auditing every sharing mechanism built on top of the looser default
Private is required by Salesforce for any object that uses record types
Record types cannot function unless OWD is set to Private
Sales reps are legally barred from seeing their own records under any other setting
questions.explain: Starting restrictive and widening deliberately is the safer direction, because loosening an OWD later is low-risk, while tightening it later is a breaking change that forces re-examining every sharing rule built on the old, looser default.

questions.prompt: Match each Financial Services Cloud household relationship type (from the Meridian Wealth Advisors case) to what it links.
right: Links a household's members to other contacts
The view for navigating a household's full set of linked relationships
Links a household Account to its individual members
Links a household Account to a business or trust Account
questions.explain: Account-Contact Relationships link a household to its members; Account-Account Relationships link a household to related businesses or trusts; Contact-Contact Relationships link household members to other contacts; and the Actionable Relationship Center is the view for navigating all of these links together.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a Salesforce Field Service scheduling policy, a ________ is a hard filter — a candidate that fails it is removed from consideration entirely, unlike a service objective, which only scores candidates relative to each other.
questions.explain: A work rule is a hard filter in a scheduling policy — for example, a technician without the required certification is removed from consideration outright, rather than merely scored lower the way a soft service objective like travel-time efficiency would be.

questions.prompt: In the Renwick Outdoor Gear portal case, why would giving the consumer audience a Partner-tier Experience Cloud license be the wrong choice, given their task list was only viewing their own Case, submitting a claim, and reading Knowledge articles?
options: It would license a narrow self-service task list at a cost tier built for deeper CRM access they don't need
Partner licenses cannot access Knowledge articles under any configuration
Consumers are not permitted to hold any Experience Cloud license
Partner-tier licenses do not support sharing sets
questions.explain: The consumer audience's entire task list fits a narrower, lower-cost Customer-tier license. Buying Partner-tier capability for that audience over-licenses the population at a cost built for deeper CRM access (Leads, Opportunities) the consumers never needed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the quote-to-cash chain in the Veltrix Software subscription-billing case.
options: CPQ is the system of record for the negotiated quote — products, discounts, and approved pricing
A billing system is authoritative for what actually gets invoiced and collected over the life of the subscription
The invoice mismatch Veltrix experienced was caused by CPQ calculating the wrong price
A manual re-keying handoff between CPQ and the billing system, with no check that the values matched, was the actual root cause of the mismatch
Usage-based billing can be treated as identical to flat-fee subscription billing, just with a different number
questions.explain: CPQ is authoritative for the quote, and billing is authoritative for ongoing invoicing and collection — two different systems of record in the same chain. The mismatch wasn't a CPQ calculation error; it came from the unchecked manual handoff into billing. Usage-based billing is a genuinely different architecture problem, not just a different price, since it requires a usage-ingestion path CPQ's flat-fee model never needed.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the quote-to-cash chain, as this course describes it, in order from the initial sales quote through to an active subscription's ongoing lifecycle.
items: CPQ captures the negotiated quote — products, discounts, and approved pricing
A contract or order record captures what was actually agreed and signed
The billing system generates invoices and collects payment over time
Amendments and renewals update the active subscription without re-running the original quote from scratch
questions.explain: The chain runs from the negotiated quote (CPQ) to the signed agreement (contract/order) to ongoing invoicing (billing), and only after a subscription is active does its amendment-and-renewal lifecycle begin — each stage building on, rather than replacing, the one before it.

questions.prompt: Why does the Harlow Community Partners nonprofit case use the Program Management Module (PMM) on top of NPSP, rather than forcing program tracking into NPSP's existing gift-and-donation object shape?
options: PMM adds objects (Programs, Program Engagements, Service Deliveries) built for a different question — who received what service and was it delivered — than NPSP's donor-focused model answers
NPSP cannot store Contact records for program clients at all
PMM replaces NPSP entirely and the two cannot be used together
Program tracking and donor tracking are legally required to be kept in separate Salesforce orgs
questions.explain: NPSP's model answers who gave what and when; PMM's Programs, Program Engagements, and Service Deliveries answer who received what service and whether it was delivered — different questions needing different objects, even though PMM is built to sit on top of NPSP's existing Contact and Account model rather than duplicating it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Ferro Holdings multi-business-unit case, a ________ field tags which business unit a record belongs to for reporting and as a sharing-rule criterion, but by itself does nothing to restrict who can see the record.
questions.explain: A business-unit field is useful for reporting and filtering, and as the criterion a sharing rule can key off of — but it enforces nothing about access on its own. Without a sharing rule (or record type plus sharing rule) built on top of it, a sufficiently open OWD would let any rep see every unit's records.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce Field Service object or concept from the Castellan HVAC case to what it represents.
right: The named combination of work rules and weighted service objectives the optimizer runs against
The job itself — what needs doing, for which customer
A technician, with their skills, territory, and calendar, eligible to be scheduled
A specific scheduled visit tied to a Work Order
questions.explain: The Work Order is the job itself; the Service Appointment is the specific scheduled visit tied to it; the Service Resource is the technician who might be assigned; and the Scheduling Policy is the named combination of work rules and weighted service objectives the optimizer evaluates against all of them.

questions.prompt: In this course's requirements-extraction method, what is an assumption, as distinct from a stated requirement?
options: A stated, checkable need that a design can be verified true or false against
Something a design relies on without explicit confirmation from the stakeholder
A named technology or mechanism presented before the underlying need has been separately stated
A risk that has already materialized into an actual failure
questions.explain: An assumption is a belief a design is quietly standing on that hasn't been explicitly confirmed with the stakeholder — which is exactly why Lesson 11 says it should be written down and challenged rather than left invisible.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a requirement, not an assumption. A requirement is the stated, checkable need itself; an assumption is a separate, unconfirmed belief the design depends on in order to satisfy that requirement. Conflating the two is exactly the mistake Lesson 9 warns against.

questions.prompt: Put these five parts of a design presentation in the order this course teaches them.
items: The problem, stated as the stakeholder experiences it
The requirement, extracted and stated specifically enough to check a design against
The alternatives considered, scored on explicit tradeoff dimensions
The recommended design, at a level of detail matched to the audience
The open risks and assumptions, presented as actively managed, not hidden
questions.explain: The five-part structure runs problem, requirement, alternatives, recommended design, then open risks and assumptions — opening on the recommended design before the problem is stated (skipping straight to step 4) is this course's named most common presentation failure.

questions.prompt: This course's mock review board names five categories of panel questions. Select every one that this course specifically describes as a "boundary question" — about the edges of a design rather than its center.
options: "What breaks this at scale?"
"Why not the alternative?"
"What did you deliberately not solve?"
"Who disagrees with you, and why might they be right?"
questions.explain: "What breaks this at scale," "what did you deliberately not solve," and "who disagrees with you" all probe the boundaries of a design — its limits, exclusions, and strongest counterargument. "Why not the alternative" is one of the five panel-question categories too, but this course specifically groups the other three as the boundary-focused set, distinct from the tradeoff-restatement that "why not the alternative" asks for.

questions.prompt: What does this course's feedback-triage method mean by "acknowledged-and-declined," as distinct from simply dismissing feedback?
options: The reviewer's concern was considered on its merits, the design stands as presented, and the reasoning for declining is stated explicitly on the record
The feedback is ignored outright with no written response
The reviewer is told their concern doesn't count because of their role
It is identical to dismissing feedback, just phrased more politely
questions.explain: Acknowledged-and-declined finishes the hypothesis test with a recorded answer: the concern was genuinely evaluated, and the reasoning for standing by the original design is written down explicitly, which is what separates it from simply brushing the feedback aside.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is a running, dated record of what was decided, why, what alternatives were rejected, and what assumptions a decision depended on — built for a later reader rather than one specific audience in one specific room.
questions.explain: A decision log is a different artifact from a presentation deck: a deck is optimized to persuade a specific audience at a specific moment, while a decision log is maintained for someone reading it later, possibly months on, trying to understand why the system works the way it does.

questions.prompt: Match each term from this course's requirements-extraction method to its definition.
right: A possible future event that would be bad if it happened, independent of any specific assumption
A named mechanism presented before the underlying need has been separately stated, foreclosing alternatives
A stated, checkable need a design can be verified against
Something a design relies on without explicit stakeholder confirmation
questions.explain: A requirement is a stated, checkable need. An assumption is an unconfirmed belief the design depends on. A solution disguised as a requirement names a mechanism before the underlying need is separately stated. A risk is a possible bad future event, independent of any particular assumption — four distinct categories this course insists on keeping separate.

questions.prompt: Per this course's portfolio-readiness checklist, why is a case study that presents its chosen design as having no downsides actually a weaker portfolio piece, not a cleaner one?
options: An experienced reviewer knows every real design involves tradeoffs, so a case with no stated risk or alternative reads as less credible, not more
Portfolio pieces are scored purely on word count
Reviewers always prefer the shortest possible case write-up
Risks and assumptions are irrelevant to technical hiring decisions
questions.explain: The checklist specifically requires naming at least one risk or assumption and showing a real alternative that was considered — a case presented as flawless signals under-examined reasoning to an experienced reviewer, not stronger work.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about this course's five tradeoff dimensions for comparing alternative designs.
options: Fit to the stated requirement is the dimension most at risk of being lost once a design becomes technically interesting
Risk and blast radius asks what happens if the design turns out to be wrong and how contained the damage would be
Two designs almost always dominate each other on every dimension at once, making comparison straightforward
Flexibility for known future change means flexibility in the abstract, regardless of whether that future change is actually likely
"Which design is better" cannot be meaningfully answered until the relative importance of the dimensions has been settled for that specific stakeholder
questions.explain: Fit to the requirement is explicitly named as easy to lose track of; risk/blast radius asks about the cost and containment of being wrong; and 'which is better' is unanswerable until priorities among dimensions are settled. Two designs rarely dominate on every dimension at once — that's the normal, not the rare, case — and flexibility is scored for a change that's actually likely, not flexibility in the abstract.

questions.prompt: Put this course's four requirements-extraction questions in the order they're meant to be asked.
items: Who said this, and what are they actually experiencing?
What would "fixed" look like, concretely, to that person?
What's being assumed that hasn't been said out loud?
Is there a solution hiding inside the ask?
questions.explain: The method starts by finding whose actual experience is behind the vague ask, then asks what a concrete fixed outcome looks like to that person, then surfaces unstated assumptions, and finally checks whether a specific solution was named before the underlying need was ever separately stated.

questions.prompt: This course's wrap-up lesson names one pattern recurring across all eight Chapter 1 case studies. What is it?
options: Separating what shape a thing takes from who gets to see or touch it, and not letting a vague request's phrasing stand in for the specific, checkable requirement underneath it
Every case was ultimately solved using the exact same Salesforce configuration
Every case required purchasing a new Salesforce license tier
Every case was resolved without ever involving a business stakeholder
questions.explain: Record type vs. sharing rule, license tier vs. sharing set, business-unit field vs. sharing rule, work rule vs. service objective, system of record vs. handoff, program model vs. donor model, household structure vs. Action Plan enforcement — eight domains, one repeated architectural habit: separate shape from visibility, and extract the real requirement before treating a vague ask as if it were one.
